summary: Mission Builder is a web game that lets students aged 10 to 20 design, launch, and run a complete space mission. Players choose why they are going to space, set a mission goal, build a spacecraft from parts and science instruments, then pick an orbit and a rocket. Six live meters (mass, power, budget, data, communications, and mission time) change with every choice, and a Launch Check shows whether the spacecraft fits the rocket and orbit. A simulation with random events tests the design, and a final report scores the mission and explains in plain language why it succeeded or failed. Three difficulty levels and helpful tooltips make it friendly for beginners. Up to four players can collaborate in team mode, and a glossary and crossword build space vocabulary. Inspired by NASA’s Why Go to Space page, it turns abstract engineering trade-offs into hands-on learning.
details:
What it does and how it works
Mission Builder is a web game where players design and run a complete space mission. They pick a purpose (benefit humanity, advance science, or inspire and unite) and a goal, build a spacecraft from structure, power, communications, and computer parts plus science instruments, and then choose an orbit and a rocket. Six live meters (mass, power, budget, data, communications, and mission time) update with every choice, so players see how one decision affects everything else. A Launch Check tells them whether the spacecraft fits the chosen rocket and orbit. A simulation then runs the mission, including random events that need quick decisions, and a final report scores the mission and explains in plain language why it succeeded or failed. [In team mode, up to four players take different roles (Mission Commander, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Communications and Resources Officer), suggest changes, and vote.]

Benefits
Players learn real mission-design thinking by doing it: every part adds capability but costs mass, power, money, or data. Mistakes are safe and instructive, because warnings explain what is wrong and what to try next. Three difficulty levels let beginners and experienced players both enjoy it. [A Mission Glossary and crossword puzzles build the vocabulary, with crossword rewards feeding back into the game.]

Intended impact
We want students aged 10 to 20 to understand that space missions are the result of trade-offs and teamwork, not magic, and to feel what it is like to be a mission engineer. By connecting each mission to a purpose, inspired by NASA’s “Why Go to Space,” the game also shows why exploration matters, which we hope encourages more young people to explore STEM careers.

Tools and technologies
We designed the interface in Google Stitch, built the working web app in Google AI Studio (HTML, CSS, JavaScript/React), and used Claude to plan the game rules and write our design and build prompts. Progress and scores are stored in the browser, so no login is needed.

Creativity
The game turns abstract engineering into a playful, colourful experience with a mascot, sticker-style design, random events, and a “Why It Matters” score that rewards missions for serving their purpose, not just for passing technical checks. [The crossword generator creates a new puzzle every time from the glossary.]

Factors we considered
We prioritised being easy to use for ages 10 to 20 (tooltips, plain-language warnings, a Cadet mode with a starter design), accuracy and honesty (all numbers are simplified game values, clearly labelled as not real NASA specifications), accessibility (large text, icons beside colours), and the challenge’s key requirements: realistic trade-offs, resource management, compatibility checks, a simulation with feedback, difficulty levels, and collaboration. NASA’s Why Go to Space, Spaceships and Rockets, and Communicating with Missions pages inspired the purpose cards and learning content, with credits in the app.
